item.title: International Criminal Court limits Afghanistan investigation to Taliban crimes
item.description:
International Criminal Court limits Afghanistan investigation to Taliban crimes
Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnelByMOLLY QUELL Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 12:36 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel, instead limiting the probe to crimes committed by the Taliban, according to court filings released Friday.
The ruling comes as the court and 13 current and former staff members are under sanctions by the Trump administration, which is opposed to any investigation into American citizens or U.S. allies, such as Israel.
The decision, which was issued Thursday but only made public on Friday, cites “significant limitations to the Prosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence” in the case. It does not elaborate.
The court's prosecutor's office told The Associated Press it has already appealed the decision.
It is not clear if the decision will mitigate Washington's attacks on the court. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to “dismantle the ICC — brick by brick, if necessary." The United States is not a member of the court and does not recognize its jurisdiction.

item.title: Hundreds of roaming cows wreak havoc in North Macedonian town, frustrating farmers
item.description:
Hundreds of roaming cows wreak havoc in North Macedonian town, frustrating farmers
Residents of Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia are dealing with a herd of over 1,000 roaming cattleByKONSTANTIN TESTORIDES Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 11:17 AM
Share
KRIVA PALANKA, North Macedonia -- They descend from the surrounding hills, mostly at night, chomping their way through gardens and crops to satiate their hunger.
For years, residents of Kriva Palanka, a farming town of about 19,000 people in northeastern North Macedonia, have struggled with a herd of roaming cattle that has grown to more than 1,000 animals, destroying property and threatening their livelihood.
It's not just crops. The wandering cows pose a serious risk to the town's water supply and to drivers on a road that leads to neighboring Bulgaria, residents say.
Many fault the country's bureaucratic maze for failing to enforce a 2024 Food and Veterinary Agency order to seize the herd from their three owners.
And even when authorities took legal action against one of the owners, bureaucratic failures derailed the case and allowed the owner to walk free, Kriva Palanka Mayor Sashko Mitovski said.
Mitovski said residents have had enough and are staging protests to urge authorities to take action.
He is asking the conservative government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski to declare a 30-day state of emergency in the municipality for authorities to resolve the bovine problem once and for all.
“The number of cattle has increased from 400 four years ago to more than 1,000 today,” Mitovski told The Associated Press.
“We convened a crisis management headquarters because we concluded that, for years, none of the responsible institutions had shown either the willingness, commitment or capacity and resources to resolve the problem.”
Pensioner Lazo Stamenkovski, 71, who lives on the town's outskirts, said the cattle have destroyed more than 150 trees in his orchard.

item.title: UK police launch sex offense investigation into author, TV personality David Walliams
item.description:
UK police launch sex offense investigation into author, TV personality David Walliams
London police say they are investigating children’s author and TV personality David Walliams for serious sexual offenses after news outlets reported allegations of misconductByBRIAN MELLEY Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 11:16 AM
LONDON -- London police said Friday that they are investigating children’s author and TV personality David Walliams for serious sexual offenses after news outlets reported that he used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex.
The Metropolitan Police said it had received a number of allegations of past abuse following the joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian newspaper.
One woman said in the reports that she was sexually assaulted by Walliams at his London home when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens.
Police are investigating different allegations than those reported by the news outlets, but said they will look into the news stories for any evidence of other crimes.
Walliams, 55, has denied the allegations, saying he had not broken any laws and was not a sexual predator.
“I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me,” Walliams said in writing to ITV and the Guardian. “Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”
Walliams is best known as the co-creator and co-star in “Little Britain,” a hugely popular TV comedy sketch show in the 2000s, but he’s also a celebrated children’s book author with some 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website.

item.title: Wife of jailed ex-leader of Northern Ireland's largest pro-UK party put on sex offenders register
item.description:
Wife of jailed ex-leader of Northern Ireland's largest pro-UK party put on sex offenders register
Eleanor Donaldson, the wife of former Northern Ireland unionist leader Jeffrey Donaldson, has been placed on the sex offenders register for five yearsByThe Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 8:36 AM
Share
LONDON -- The wife of Jeffrey Donaldson — the former leader of Northern Ireland’s largest unionist party who last month was sentenced to 15 years in prison for the rape and sex abuse of two girls decades ago — was placed on the sex offenders register for five years on Friday.
During her husband’s trial at Newry Crown Court, Eleanor Donaldson, 60, was found to have aided and abetted his offenses by witnessing the abuse and doing nothing to intervene. Because of mental health issues, she faced only a fact-finding hearing that couldn’t result in a conviction.
At Friday's hearing, Judge Paul Ramsey explained the court order to her when she appeared briefly on a remote link. She appeared on the link with her lawyer and kept her eyes closed and her head bowed as the judge addressed her.
As well as being put on the sex offenders register, she was given a three-year supervision and treatment order.
Being on the sex offenders register will require Donaldson to comply with strict reporting and lifestyle rules managed by the police.
Both of the victims in the case were in court on Friday.
Jeffrey Donaldson, 63, was one of Northern Ireland's best-known politicians until his arrest stunned his political colleagues and wider society two years ago.

item.title: Bus and truck collision in India's Assam state kills at least 24 people
item.description:
Bus and truck collision in India's Assam state kills at least 24 people
A bus has collided with a container truck in Assam, India, killing at least 24 people and injuring 11 othersByWASBIR HUSSAIN Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 8:32 AM
GUWAHATI, India -- A bus collided with a container truck in the northeastern Indian state of Assam on Friday, killing at least 24 people and 11 injuring others, authorities said.
The crash occurred on a highway near Kaziranga National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site renowned for its one-horned rhinos, about 225 kilometers (140 miles) east of the state capital, Dispur. Children and the bus driver were among the dead, officials said.
State minister Atul Bora described the crash as one of the worst in Assam’s history and said police were investigating the cause of the collision. Bora said witnesses reported that the bus was speeding before the crash.

item.title: Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as US-led talks consider Europe security
item.description:
Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as US-led talks consider Europe security
Ukraine has launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russian targets in one of its largest aerial attacks since the invasion began almost five years agoBySAMYA KULLAB Associated Press and HANNA ARHIROVA Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 7:01 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow’s invasion nearly five years ago.
Meanwhile, U.S. and Russian negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That change, long sought by Moscow, has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark over NATO’s future role.
“Russia wants to talk about questions of European security architecture. We don’t need to talk about that. There is one,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, referring to the NATO military alliance.
After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys went in person to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was meeting with European leaders in Dublin, Ireland.
Further talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Kushner said Russia has agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow's long insistence that the continent’s governments should be excluded because they were part of the problem by supporting Ukraine.
Europe’s presence at the negotiating table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner said on X.

item.title: Charity-run kitchens in Havana feed a growing number of Cubans as crisis deepens
item.description:
Charity-run kitchens in Havana feed a growing number of Cubans as crisis deepens
Hundreds of people line up each night outside a charity-run food pantry in Havana, hoping for their only meal of the dayByANDREA RODRÍGUEZ Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 5:01 AM
Share
HAVANA -- Every night, hundreds of people line up outside a charity-run food pantry in the heart of Havana, some sleeping on the sidewalk as they wait for what may be their only meal of the day.
When the doors open at 7 a.m., people hurry inside carrying numbered plastic containers. With so many mouths to feed, volunteers follow a carefully organized routine: They wash the containers, call out the numbers and hand out portions of food.
“We’re having a really rough time,” said Fernando Fernández, a 71-year-old retiree who regularly visits the Asociación Quisicuaba, a group that runs a community kitchen in Havana. “I have to arrive in the early morning. Sometimes I even have to get in line the day before.”
Fernández, a former cook and security guard, is among a growing number of Cubans struggling to feed themselves as the country’s prolonged economic crisis deepens, worsened by U.S. energy restrictions, inflation and dwindling government resources.
As the state struggles to provide subsidized food, charity-run kitchens and food pantries have become a lifeline for vulnerable Cubans, including retired doctors, teachers and former government workers. Supported by religious groups, international aid organizations and the United Nations, they provide what for many is their only reliable hot meal.
Centers such as Quisicuaba, often housed in religious buildings or affiliated with faith-based groups, have proliferated across the island in recent years.
Fernández, a former caretaker, once visited the soup kitchen with his 80-year-old wife, Josefa, but now goes alone because she is ill. The couple survives on her monthly pension of 3,200 Cuban pesos, a little more than $3, and assistance from Quisicuaba. ...

item.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a US radar in Bahrain, and other Mideast news
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a US radar in Bahrain, and other Mideast news
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, marking the first such claim in monthsByThe Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 3:08 AM
Share
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, the first such claim in months. The Guard also said a tanker struck a mine while trying to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, causing an explosion.
Neither claim could be independently verified.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.
A report by Iran's official IRNA news agency quoted a statement by the Guard as saying the attack on the U.S. radar system followed a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the southern Iranian port of Sirik.
Bahrain has been one of the strongest critics of Iran and is home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet.
The statement said the attack on the radar was a serious warning to the U.S. to cease its strikes. It was the first report by Iran on targeting a facility in Bahrain since September.
During an air war that began in February, Iran targeted U.S. bases in neighboring Arab nations including Bahrain in retaliation for U.S. strikes. Since then, Iran routinely targets oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for international oil shipments.
U.S. Central Command and Bahrain's Ministry of Information did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Nauru's president has no political opponents after all lawmakers joined the government side
item.description:
Nauru's president has no political opponents after all lawmakers joined the government side
Nauru’s president, David Adeang, has announced that all opposition lawmakers in parliament have joined his governmentByCHARLOTTE GRAHAM-MCLAY Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 2:36 AM
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- Nauru’s president, David Adeang, has said all opposition lawmakers in parliament have joined his government, a move he said reflected “unity, stability and shared purpose” in the Pacific Island country’s politics.
The unusual move leaves the 19-member parliament without any political opposition. While it’s common for island countries in the South Pacific Ocean to take fluid approaches to forming government and opposition blocs or for lawmakers to switch between them, political debate is habitually robust and Nauru is rare in having no opposing politicians at all.
In a Facebook post Tuesday, Adeang didn’t explain what had prompted the change beyond a “shared commitment” to put Nauru's interests first. He also didn’t suggest who would supply the scrutiny usually provided by opponents in a country with a single house of parliament.
“There will still be a diversity of views and robust debate as in any strong and healthy democracy,” Adeang wrote.
The appointment of two lawmakers, Pyon Deiye and Jason Bingham Agir, as deputy cabinet ministers meant that Nauru’s parliament was in total support of the government for the first time since the country’s independence in 1968, Adeang said.
Government Facebook posts announcing the change were the sole source of information about it; all news outlets in the country of 12,000 people are government-owned. Foreign reporters are discouraged from traveling there, with journalist visa applications priced at 8,000 Australian dollars ($5,445).
Adeang made global news headlines in August when he said his country would officially become known as Naoero, making it the latest state to formally adopt the local spelling of its name. ...

item.title: Pakistan's army says it killed 74 militants in raids on their hideouts
item.description:
Pakistan's army says it killed 74 militants in raids on their hideouts
Pakistani security forces have killed 74 militants in raids on hideouts in regions bordering Afghanistan over the past 10 days, according to the militaryByThe Associated PressNovember 13, 2026, 1:46 AM
ISLAMABAD -- Pakistani security forces have killed 74 militants in multiple raids on hideouts in the northwest and southwestern regions bordering Afghanistan over the past 10 days, the military said Friday.
The raids were carried out in the Mir Ali and Orakzai districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the military said in a statement. Troops killed 43 militants and seized weapons, ammunition and explosive devices, the statement said.
Separately, troops killed 31 militants in multiple operations in Balochistan province, the site of a bloody insurgency led by the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, since Nov. 3, the military said. It alleged the militants were backed by Afghanistan and India. Kabul and New Delhi have previously denied such allegations.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif praised the security forces and vowed to continue the fight against militancy.
